Andreolepis.note: Scales and teeth from the late Silurian of Gotland and Russia that belong near the root of all bony fishes, four hundred and twenty-five million years old.

Appendisphaera.note: A spiny acritarch of the early Ediacaran seas, one of the zone fossils of the Doushantuo-Pertatataka palynoflora; possibly the resting cysts of early animals.

Arctinurus.note: A lichid the size of a dinner plate from the Rochester Shale of New York, one of the largest Silurian trilobites.

Asaphellus.note: A smooth Tremadocian asaphid of the cool Gondwanan shelves -- Argentina, Bolivia, Morocco, Bohemia, Wales -- and of Kazakhstan.

Aspidella.note: The holdfast disc of Newfoundland's Fermeuse Formation, the first Ediacaran fossil ever named (1872) and dismissed for a century; thousands cover some bedding planes.

Atar Group microfossils.note: The cherts and shales of the Atar and El Mreiti groups of the Taoudeni basin of Mauritania, about 1.1 billion years old: cyanobacterial mats, colonial cells and the cysts of early eukaryotes, on a shallow sea over the West African craton.

Beothukis.note: A spindle-shaped rangeomorph of Mistaken Point, its self-similar branches all on one face, that lay flat on the deep-sea mud in the dark.

Billingsella.note: An early hinged brachiopod of the late Cambrian, found on every continent's shelf, from a family near the root of the orthides.

Birkenia.note: A small anaspid of the Silurian of Lesmahagow and Norway, deep-bodied and scaled, with a tail that bent downward: an early jawless fish that swam in open water.

Bumastus.note: A smooth illaenid of the Wenlock reefs of Dudley and Gotland and the Silurian of Laurentia, its head and tail nearly featureless domes.

Cambropallas.note: A trilobite a hand-span long from the Cambrian of Morocco, the commonest large fossil of the Jbel Wawrmast beds and of the fossil trade.

Catenipora.note: A chain coral: tubes joined side by side into ranks that wander across the rock like chain-link, on Late Ordovician and Silurian shelves everywhere.

Chuaria.note: A carbonaceous disc a few millimetres across, among the commonest large fossils of the Proterozoic, from the Grand Canyon to the Vindhyan of India: the compressed remains of a large-celled eukaryote or a colony.

Climatius.note: A spiny 'shark' of the Old Red Sandstone of Scotland, a hand long, with paired rows of fin spines under its belly.

Colpocoryphe.note: A calymenid of the Armorican, Iberian, Bohemian and Moroccan Ordovician, found rolled up by the hundred in the quartzites of Brittany.

Conocoryphe.note: A blind trilobite of the Cambrian mud floors of Bohemia, the Montagne Noire, Spain, Wales and Morocco: eyes were of no use in the dark water it lived in.

Cordylodus.note: The conodont of the Cambrian-Ordovician boundary: its species define the last Cambrian and the first Ordovician zones on every continent.

Cyclocrinites.note: A golf-ball alga: a sphere of packed branch-tips a few centimetres across, calcified, in Ordovician and Silurian limestones of Laurentia and Baltica.

Cyclomedusa.note: Concentric discs pressed into Ediacaran sandstones on every continent, named as a jellyfish and now read as the holdfasts of fronds and the marks of microbial colonies.

Cyrtograptus.note: A spiral graptolite throwing off side branches, the zone fossil of the Wenlock in Britain, Bohemia, Baltica and Arctic Canada.

Dalmanitina.note: A phacopid with a pointed tail that lived through the Hirnantian glaciation: the trilobite of the cold-water Hirnantia fauna from Bohemia and Wales to Morocco and Bolivia.

Dicellograptus.note: Two stipes curving up like horns, the Late Ordovician graptolite of the black shales from Scotland to Kazakhstan and Australia.

Dimorphosiphon.note: A calcified green alga of the Ordovician of Baltica and Laurentia, close to the living Halimeda in build, and a rock-former in Norway's Oslo region.

Eccaparadoxides.note: A paradoxidid of the Cambrian of Bohemia, Spain, Morocco and Scandinavia, with a long spiny pygidium; a zone fossil of the middle Cambrian across the Gondwanan and Baltic shelves.

Ectillaenus.note: A smooth illaenid of the Mediterranean province, tucked into the sediment with only its convex head showing, in Bohemia, Portugal, Morocco and Wales.

Ellipsocephalus.note: A smooth-shelled trilobite of the Jince beds of Bohemia and the Cambrian of Scandinavia, the first trilobite described from Bohemia (1825).

Encrinurus.note: The strawberry-headed trilobite of Silurian reef flanks, its head covered in tubercles, from Dudley and Gotland to Laurentia, Siberia and Australia.

Entelognathus primordialis.note: A placoderm from the Kuanti Formation of Yunnan with a bony jaw of the pattern all bony fishes and land vertebrates inherit; it moved the origin of the jaws we have into the armoured fishes.

Eoandromeda.note: An eight-armed spiral a few centimetres across, in the Doushantuo shales of South China and the Ediacara sandstones of the Flinders Ranges: the same animal on two continents, and a candidate ctenophore.

Eospirifer.note: The first spiriferide: a brachiopod with a coiled internal support for its feeding organ, from the last Ordovician to the Early Devonian, the start of a line that ran to the Jurassic.

Guiyu oneiros.note: The oldest articulated bony fish, from the late Silurian Kuanti Formation of Yunnan: a lobe-finned fish with a mosaic of features the ray-fins and lobe-fins would later divide between them.

Hallopora.note: A branching trepostome bryozoan of Ordovician and Silurian shelves, its twigs the commonest bryozoan debris of the Cincinnatian.

Haootia quadriformis.note: A four-fold body with bundled fibres from the Fermeuse Formation of Newfoundland, read as the oldest animal with muscles: a stalked cnidarian.

Heterorthella.note: An orthide brachiopod of the cold Malvinokaffric seas of Silurian and Devonian Gondwana: Bolivia, Brazil, the Falklands and South Africa.

Hoekaspis.note: A large asaphid of the Darriwilian shelf of Bolivia and northern Argentina, the commonest trilobite of the Andean Ordovician.

Hupetina.note: One of the first trilobites of Morocco's Anti-Atlas, a fallotaspidoid of the Issafen Formation, near the base of the trilobite record on the Gondwanan shelf.

Hyolithes.note: The type hyolith: a cone-shaped shell with a lid, and a pair of curved struts it steered with, on sea floors from the Cambrian to the Permian.

Iapetognathus fluctivagus.note: The conodont whose first appearance at Green Point, Newfoundland, defines the base of the Ordovician.

Icriodus.note: A shallow-water conodont of the Devonian, its rows of nodes the standard zonation of the near-shore seas from the Lochkovian to the Famennian.

Inaria.note: A sac-like Ediacaran body with a lobed base, from the Flinders Ranges, read as a sea-anemone-like animal buried in life position.

Isograptus.note: Two stipes folded back on themselves: the graptolite of the Dapingian, the Isograptus victoriae zones named from Victoria and found from Newfoundland to China.

Jamoytius.note: A naked, eel-like jawless fish of the Lesmahagow Silurian of Scotland, with a ring of cartilage round its mouth: a lamprey's kin or something older.

Jujuyaspis.note: The olenid that marks the base of the Ordovician in Argentina and Bolivia, Oaxaca, Nevada, Kazakhstan and Norway: a wide-ranging trilobite of the outer shelf.

Kainella.note: A Tremadocian trilobite with a broad spiny pygidium, of the Argentine Cordillera Oriental, the Tinu Formation of Oaxaca and the Laurentian shelf.

Lichenaria.note: The first tabulate coral: small colonies of prismatic tubes in Early Ordovician limestones of Laurentia and Siberia, before reefs had corals.

Lingulella.note: A small tongue-shaped phosphatic brachiopod of Cambrian and Ordovician shelves, burrowing like its living cousin Lingula.

Loganellia.note: A thelodont preserved whole in the Silurian of Scotland: a flattened jawless fish with a forked tail and, unexpectedly, gill-pouch denticles.

Megasphaera.note: Phosphatised spheres of dividing cells from the Doushantuo Formation of Guizhou, argued for twenty years to be animal embryos and by others to be giant bacteria or algae.

Miaohe biota.note: The black shales at the top of the Doushantuo Formation: carbonaceous seaweeds by the dozen, the spiral Eoandromeda, tubes and worm-like forms, a quiet late Ediacaran sea floor in South China.

Mixopterus.note: A eurypterid with a scorpion-like curled tail and spined forelimbs, from the Ringerike sandstones of Norway; it walked as much as it swam.

Namapoikia.note: An encrusting skeletal organism up to a metre across that lined fissures in the Nama Group reefs of Namibia: the largest of the first animals with mineral skeletons.

Nasepia.note: An erniettomorph of the Nama Group, a bag of tubular segments that lived half-buried in the shifting sand of the last Ediacaran shelves.

Nemagraptus gracilis.note: A slender S-shaped graptolite whose first appearance defines the base of the Sandbian; found on every Late Ordovician shelf and ocean floor.

Nisusia.note: A kutorginid brachiopod of the Burgess Shale and the Laurentian shelf, sometimes preserved with its spines still attached.

Normalograptus.note: The plain single-stiped graptolite that outlived the Hirnantian ice: Normalograptus persculptus names the last Ordovician zone and its kin the first of the Silurian.

Ogygiocaris.note: A flat, wide asaphid of the Ogygiocaris shale of the Oslo region, the trilobite of the Baltic Darriwilian mud floors.

Onnia.note: A trinucleid with a wide pitted fringe, named for the Onny valley of Shropshire and sold by the thousand from the Ordovician of Morocco.

Orthis.note: The orthide that named its order: a ribbed, straight-hinged brachiopod of Ordovician shelves from Baltica and Laurentia to the Gondwanan margin.

Ozarkodina.note: The commonest conodont of Silurian seas, whose apparatus is known entire; its species date the Silurian on every shelf.

Palaeopascichnus.note: Chains of repeating chambers on Ediacaran bedding planes, once taken for a trail and now for the body of a giant protist growing chamber by chamber, worldwide.

Palaeoporella.note: A calcified dasyclad of Late Ordovician and Silurian shelves, one of the algae that turned Silurian lagoons into limestone.

Parabolina.note: An olenid trilobite of the Furongian black shales -- the Alum Shale of Scandinavia, Wales, Argentina and Oaxaca -- living at the edge of oxygen on the sea floor.

Pectinifrons.note: A comb-shaped rangeomorph of Mistaken Point, a row of branches rising from a basal stolon, thousands preserved by volcanic ash on one surface.

Placoparia.note: A blind cheirurid with a broad gently rounded shield, of the muddy cold-water shelves of Bohemia, Iberia, Morocco and Wales on the Gondwanan side of the Rheic Ocean.

Prasopora.note: A gumdrop-shaped trepostome bryozoan of the Trenton and Cincinnatian limestones, and of Baltica: the bryozoan that built the Late Ordovician sea floor's small mounds.

Protospongia.note: A thin-walled glass sponge whose cross-shaped spicules lie in rows, in Cambrian and Ordovician shales from the Burgess Shale to Wales and China.

Rasthof microbialites.note: The cap carbonate laid over the Sturtian glacial deposits of the Otavi Group of Namibia: roll-up microbial mats metres thick, the first life of the sea floor after the snowball ice withdrew.

Rhabdinopora.note: The first graptolite to leave the sea floor: a conical net of branches hanging from a float, drifting over every Tremadocian sea.

Saetograptus.note: A Ludlow monograptid with paired spines on each cup, the zone fossil of the late Silurian shales of Wales, Bohemia and the Baltic.

Selenopeltis.note: A spiny odontopleurid whose long pleural spines swept back the length of its body: the emblem of the Ordovician Mediterranean province, from Bohemia and Morocco to Wales and Turkey.

Shaanxilithes.note: A ribbon-shaped fossil with fine transverse rings, from the last Ediacaran of Shaanxi and India to the first Cambrian: an animal or a colony, and a marker of the boundary interval.

Sowerbyella.note: A small, finely ribbed strophomenide lying flat on Ordovician and Silurian mud floors worldwide, often in shell beds by the thousand.

Strophomena.note: A wide, gently curved strophomenide with a straight hinge, resting on the sediment on its convex valve, on every Ordovician and Silurian shelf.

Syringopora.note: The organ-pipe coral: loose bundles of tubes joined by cross-bars, from the Silurian to the Permian on every continent, common in Carboniferous reefs.

Tanarium.note: A large acritarch with long branching processes, a signature of the early Ediacaran plankton after the Marinoan ice, from South China to central Australia and Siberia.

Tawuia.note: A sausage-shaped carbonaceous compression a centimetre long, found with Chuaria in Tonian and Ediacaran shales worldwide; read as a macroalga or a coenocytic organism.

Tetragraptus.note: Four stipes from one point, a Floian graptolite of the open ocean whose species date the early Ordovician worldwide.

Thelodus.note: A jawless fish covered in tiny tooth-like scales, known mostly from those scales, which pave Silurian sandstones from the Baltic to Arctic Canada and Siberia.

Trepassia.note: A rangeomorph frond of the Drook Formation of Newfoundland, among the oldest large animals known at about 574 million years.

Trinucleus.note: The fringed trilobite of the Welsh Ordovician, blind, its pitted brim thought to sense currents in the mud it ploughed.

Vendia.note: A small segmented Ediacaran of the White Sea, a centimetre long, with the offset left-right quilting of Dickinsonia's kin; the genus that named the Vendian.

Vermiporella.note: A calcified dasyclad alga, a branching tube a few millimetres wide, that paved shallow Ordovician and Silurian carbonate floors on every continent.
